Who runs property tax in Philadelphia County

Everything runs through city government. The county has had the same borders as the city since the consolidation of 1854, and the county offices were folded into city government in 1952, so there is no separate county tax bill or county treasurer to call.

Three city bodies share the work. The Office of Property Assessment sets the value of every parcel. Bills and collections for the Real Estate Tax come from the Department of Revenue. The Board of Revision of Taxes hears formal appeals of those values.

The county has 1,574,281 residents and 764,829 housing units. Owned homes have a typical value of $243,100, and roughly 51.8 percent of households are owners, which leaves nearly half as renters. Those figures are countywide, so a rowhouse in one neighborhood can sit far from the middle.

How a house is assessed

An assessor weighs a house's size, age, location and condition against recent nearby sales of similar homes. Their inputs include field inspections, aerial photos, permit and deed data from other city departments, and listing and sales data.

New Notices of Valuation go out in late June for the following tax year, and the 2027 round covered more than 580,000 properties. The City's own estimate was a bill change of about $97 for the median-valued home, though any single house can land well above or below that. A notice is not a bill. If none arrives, either your market value did not change or the office has an old mailing address for you.

New values take effect January 1 of the tax year. Bills for that year go out the December before and fall due on March 31.

Tax rate and due date

For tax year 2025 the City published a total rate of 1.3998 percent of assessed value: 0.6159 percent for the City and 0.7839 percent for the school district. The bill is due March 31 each year.

A late payment picks up a charge of 1.5 percent a month beginning April 1. Tax still unpaid on the next January 1 draws an addition of up to 15 percent. The account is then registered delinquent, a lien is filed for the full amount, and the City may start the sheriff sale process. Further interest and fees land on January 1 and February 1 once the account turns delinquent.

Owners can pay on the Philadelphia Tax Center, over the phone, by check to a Philadelphia post office box, or at the Municipal Services Building and the North and Northeast Philadelphia satellite offices. Ask the Department of Revenue for the current box number and office hours before you go.

How to appeal your assessment

Start with a First Level Review at the Office of Property Assessment, then, or instead, file a formal appeal with the Board of Revision of Taxes. Formal appeals are due the first Monday in October ahead of the tax year they affect, so a 2028 value is challenged in October 2027.

Assessment cycle in Philadelphia
StepTiming
Notices of Valuation mailed, values postedLate June
First Level ReviewDeadline printed on the notice
Board of Revision of Taxes filingFirst Monday in October
Tax bills start going outDecember
New assessments take effectJanuary 1
Payment dueMarch 31

The Board accepts appeals that show the market value is too high or too low, that the value is not uniform with similar nearby homes, or that the recorded characteristics of the property are substantially wrong. Filing is by mail, email or in person at 601 Walnut Street, Suite 325 East, and hearings can be held in person or by video. Notice of the hearing arrives about 45 to 90 days ahead.

Two late-filing exceptions help buyers. A new owner who takes a deed between the first Monday of October and December 31 has 30 days from the deed, and a buyer who signs an agreement of sale in that window has 30 days from signing.

Relief programs

People who live in the house have the most options, and most of them reduce the balance long before a sale is on the table.

  • Homestead Exemption: $100,000 comes off the taxable assessment of an owner-occupied home in 2027, compared with $80,000 for 2023 bills.
  • Installment plan: seniors and income-qualified owners can spread the year's bill over monthly payments instead of a single March payment.
  • Tax freeze: senior and low-income versions hold the bill steady when rates or assessments climb later.
  • Longtime Owner Occupants Program: limits taxable value for people who have lived in the home ten or more years and face a steep jump.
  • Owner-occupied payment agreement: monthly payments on back taxes, set by household income and size.
  • An exemption for disabled service members, plus a catastrophic loss adjustment when damage cuts value by 50 percent or more.

Separately, the state offers a Property Tax/Rent Rebate program to seniors and adults with disabilities, and a Philadelphia district office answers questions about it.

Selling with taxes owed

Taxes are the seller's through the closing date. Whatever is past due gets paid out of the seller's proceeds at the settlement table. A lien follows the house into a sale, so the first thing a title company searches for is property tax, water and sewer liens.

  • Water liens can be looked up at water-lien.phila.gov, and a payoff request is emailed to the Water Department a month before settlement.
  • Realty Transfer Tax runs 4.578 percent, made up of 3.578 percent for the City and 1 percent for the Commonwealth. It is due at recording, and the two sides commonly divide it.
  • If a water lien goes unpaid it becomes the new owner's problem, so the payoff is requested before the sale.

If time is short, a cash offer on the house in its present state is an option, and the City gets paid through the title company.

What to gather before you list

A few early requests keep the settlement date from slipping.

  1. Get the parcel's current balance from the Department of Revenue, interest and fees included.
  2. Ask the Water Department for a payoff figure by email, about a month ahead of settlement.
  3. Search the parcel at water-lien.phila.gov ahead of the title company's lien search.
  4. If the account is delinquent and you live in the home, ask about an owner-occupied payment agreement before the City starts the sheriff sale process.
  5. Mention any Homestead Exemption or tax freeze to the title company, since both shape the balance.

With a cash buyer, repairs and cleanup are not part of the deal, and any tax owed is settled through the title company instead of from your own pocket.

Frequently asked questions

Does Philadelphia County have a separate county tax bill?

No. City and county cover the same ground. The Department of Revenue mails a single Real Estate Tax bill that includes both the City and the School District of Philadelphia, and it can tell you the balance on any parcel.

When is the Philadelphia County property tax due?

March 31 of each year. Bills are usually mailed in December, and monthly additions of one and a half percent begin April 1 on any open balance.

When must a formal assessment appeal be filed?

By the first Monday in October of the year before the tax year it affects. Exceptions of 30 days apply to people who bought or signed an agreement of sale late in the year.

Can the City sell my house for unpaid tax?

Yes. It can. Once January 1 of the next year passes with tax unpaid, a lien attaches and the sheriff sale process can begin. If you live in the home, ask about an owner-occupied payment agreement before that point.

Who pays the tax when I sell?

You owe the tax up to the closing date, and the title company deals with liens. Request the tax balance from Revenue and the water payoff from the Water Department well ahead of settlement.

Two offices, three bills

No single office sets the whole bill in Allegheny County. The Office of Property Assessments decides what each parcel is worth for tax purposes. The Treasurer’s Office prepares and collects only the county’s share.

Your school district and your municipality each set their own millage rate and mail their own bills. The county rate went up to 6.43 mills in 2025, which means $6.43 of tax for every $1,000 of assessed value. In 2025 the Treasurer’s Office collected more than $500 million across more than 550,000 parcels, about 45% of the county’s operating budget.

How assessments work

The county runs on base year assessments, and the base year is 2012, with a value date of January 1, 2012. The last countywide reassessment took effect for tax year 2013, and no new one has replaced it.

A house gets a new assessed value only for narrow reasons:

  • An omission, or a mathematical or clerical error.
  • A physical change such as a demolition, a subdivision or work under a building permit.
  • An interim assessment that a school district or municipality requests on new construction or major improvements.
  • A catastrophic loss, which requires an application within six months of the loss.

Values on the county’s Real Estate parcel search are base year figures plus those changes. They do not follow current prices, and a sale, even a very high one, does not change the assessment by itself.

Due dates and penalties

Bills arrive in January, and the cheapest day to pay is on or before March 31. The same calendar repeats every year, so go by the dates printed on your own bill.

Allegheny County real estate tax calendar
DateWhat happens
JanuaryAssessments are certified and tax statements are mailed
March 31Last day for the 2% discount off the gross tax
April 30Last day to pay the gross (face) amount
May 1Past due period starts: a one-time 5% penalty plus 1% interest a month
June 30Annual deadline to apply for Senior Citizen Tax Relief

The Treasurer handles the current tax year only. Anything still unpaid goes to Jordan Tax Service on January 1 of each year, and owners with delinquent or liened years should call Jordan Tax Service at 412-835-5243. Continued nonpayment can end in a Sheriff Sale of the property.

How to appeal your assessment

The first level of appeal is the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review, known as BPAAR. Its annual window runs from July 1 through September 1, so a filing after that waits for the next season.

BPAAR handles scheduling, hearing notices and postponements. Every hearing is held by telephone. Residential owners get notice at least 14 days ahead, and commercial owners at least 21 days ahead. The county has published 49.3% as the common level ratio for the 2027 tax year, applied to market value in appeals heard starting in September 2026.

  • An owner may appear alone, hire an attorney, or name an authorized representative.
  • A school district, a municipality or the county can file an appeal on the same parcel; the owner may attend but does not have to.
  • Only the party who filed can withdraw an appeal.
  • A losing party can take the BPAAR decision to the Court of Common Pleas, through the Board of Viewers.

A Special Appeal can be filed year round, but only in response to a written determination notice from the Office of Property Assessments.

Homestead and senior relief

The county lists several programs that can lower a bill. Two matter most to homeowners.

  • Act 50, the Homestead and Farmstead Exclusion, cuts a primary residence’s assessed value by $18,000 for county tax purposes only.
  • Act 77, Senior Citizen Tax Relief, gives a 30% reduction in the county bill to owners who are at least 60, earn $30,000 or less a year, and have lived in and owned the home for at least 10 years. The deadline to apply is June 30.

Other programs include Act 76 (LERTA) abatements for commercial and industrial property in some municipalities, Act 156 Clean and Green for land in farm or forest use, a Residential Visitability Design Tax Credit under Act 132, and a catastrophic loss reduction for structures that lost 50% or more of their value to fire or a natural disaster. A Volunteer Service Tax Credit rewards eligible emergency responders.

Act 50 covers primary residences only, so a house that becomes a rental falls outside it. If you sell to a landlord, the new owner’s bill will lose that $18,000 reduction.

Selling with taxes owed

The Treasurer’s real estate tax department prepares delinquent tax files and property liens. It also handles tax certification requests, which is how a closing agent checks a parcel’s county tax status before the sale. If you owe back taxes, call Jordan Tax Service for the payoff, and expect the title company to collect it from your proceeds at closing.

Property tax is separate from the transfer tax at recording, which runs from 2% to 5% depending on the municipality and school district. Ask your title company for the combined rate on your address.

New rule for investor buyers

Under Act 29 of 2026, buyers of non-owner-occupied real estate must give contact details to the county’s chief assessor within 30 days of purchase. Corporate and LLC owners must name an individual who is authorized to fix code violations, and owners have 30 days to report any change. Failing to comply, or knowingly giving false information, can bring a fine of up to $500. A seller dealing with an investor buyer may hear about this at closing.

Allegheny County housing context

The county spans 745 square miles where the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers form the Ohio, and it holds 130 municipalities. That is why local millage and transfer tax rates differ so widely from one street to the next. Population is 1,225,035 as of July 2025. About 65.2% of homes are owner-occupied, and the median value of an owner-occupied home is $227,600.

Owners with no mortgage still carry about $654 a month in selected costs, which shows how much of a household budget goes to the county bill, the school bill and the municipal bill.

What the 2012 base year means for a seller

Because the county values houses off a frozen 2012 snapshot, your assessment may sit far from what a buyer will pay. Do not expect the number on the parcel search to match your list price. A buyer who looks up the parcel will see an old figure, and the buyer’s own school and municipal bills are what move the monthly cost. If you think the figure is wrong because of an error or a change to the building, that is a reason to use the appeal route rather than wait for a reassessment.

Before you list: a short tax checklist

Learn whether you have claimed the homestead exclusion, since the buyer will not inherit it if the house becomes a rental. Check the date on your latest bill against the calendar above. If you are behind, ask for a payoff before you accept an offer, so the number does not change your net at the closing table.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a discount for paying Allegheny County property tax early?

Yes. The county gives a 2% discount off the gross tax on payments made by March 31, and the face amount is due through April 30.

What penalty applies after April 30 in Allegheny County?

Starting May 1 an unpaid bill picks up a one-time 5% penalty, then 1% interest on the gross tax for every month it stays unpaid. Past years move to Jordan Tax Service on January 1.

When is the Allegheny County appeal window?

It opens July 1 and closes September 1 each year. File through BPAAR; a later filing waits for the next annual season.

Does Allegheny County reassess a house when it sells?

No. Assessments rest on a 2012 base year, and the county changes a value only for omissions, errors, physical changes, interim requests or catastrophic loss.

Who runs the senior discount in Allegheny County?

The Treasurer's Office runs Senior Citizen Tax Relief. Applicants must be 60 or older, earn $30,000 or less, and have owned and lived in the home 10 years, with a June 30 yearly deadline.

County offices that handle property tax

Two county offices matter to a seller: the Board of Assessment Appeals, which sets values, and the Tax Claim Bureau, which pursues delinquent bills. Both sit in Norristown, the county seat.

The Board of Assessment Appeals values and assesses all real estate for county, municipal and school tax purposes. It also keeps the assessment rolls, the tax maps and the registry of who owns each parcel. The office phone is 610-278-3761. Walk-in filings are taken in Norristown on weekdays between 8:30 and 4:00, and the registry window shuts a little sooner, at 3:45.

If you are dividing a lot before a sale, you have a third contact. Lot line changes and requests for a new parcel number go to the Board's Mapping Division, reached through the same phone number or at boamapping@montgomerycountypa.gov.

The county, the municipality and the school district all use that one assessed value. For the current bill from the municipal or school side, ask the municipality or the school district, since the Board sets values and does not collect the tax.

Assessment appeal deadline

Annual appeals are due by August 1, and the same date applies to applications for real estate tax exemption. State law requires all annual appeals to be heard and acted on by October 31, and changes must reach the rolls, the owner and the taxing districts by November 15 (Title 53 Pa.C.S. section 8844).

The Board's forms page lists the documents an owner is likely to need:

  • Assessment appeal form and a separate commercial appeal procedure.
  • Assessment appeal fees schedule.
  • Homestead application, homestead appeal form and homestead removal form.
  • Exemption application and instructions.
  • Appeal rules and regulations, and a notice for appeals pending in court.
  • Mailing address change form and a list of taxing authorities.
  • A Taxpayer Relief Act document and a notice on an assessor's right to enter a property.

Watch the postmark. Mail delays can cause a timely filing to be stamped late, so ask for a hand-cancelled postmark, a certificate of mailing, registered or certified mail, or buy postage at the counter. Hand delivery to the Norristown office avoids the issue.

How the Tax Claim Bureau sells delinquent property

The Bureau can sell a parcel four ways under the Real Estate Tax Sale law. A property that has gone unsold moves along the sequence, and the buyer's liability changes at each step.

  • Upset sale: scheduled each September and December for parcels whose taxes from two years earlier are still unpaid. Buyers take the property subject to all liens.
  • Private sale: possible after a parcel has been exposed but not sold. A written bid goes to the Bureau, and anyone objecting has 45 days to petition the court.
  • Judicial sale: held at least once each year in August and December, only for exposed parcels that did not sell. Parcels are presented free and clear of liens.
  • Repository sale: for properties unsold at judicial sale, with each taxing district reviewing any bid.
Tax Claim Bureau sale types and what the buyer takes on
Sale typeWhen it is heldLiens
Upset saleSeptember and DecemberBuyer takes subject to all liens
Private saleAfter a parcel is exposed but unsoldBuyer assumes liens
Judicial saleAugust and December, at least once a yearFree and clear
Repository saleAfter a judicial sale fails to sell the parcelTaxing districts review each bid

The next dates on the calendar are a continued judicial sale and a continued upset sale on December 10, 2026. Sales are advertised in two newspapers and the Montgomery Bar Association journal within two months of the sale.

Regular mail to the Bureau goes to P.O. Box 190, Norristown, PA 19404, and overnight carriers use One Montgomery Plaza, Suite 600. Its desk is staffed on weekdays from 8:30 to 4:15. Call the Bureau for the schedule after that.

Transfer tax at closing

Usually a seller owes some, unless the transfer is exempt. The commonwealth taxes the value of the property at 1 percent, and the grantor and grantee both answer for it. The county recorder takes payment as the deed is lodged and sends the state share on, while local rates come from the municipality and school district.

Exempt transfers include certain gifts within a family, deeds to government units and estates that pass at death. Because each municipality sets its own local share, have the closing agent confirm the combined rate for your specific address rather than assume a county-wide figure.

Real estate taxes themselves are usually prorated at closing between buyer and seller as your sales contract provides. Any amount already delinquent is a separate matter, because the Tax Claim Bureau pursues those balances and the closing agent will want them settled.

Montgomery County for a seller preparing to list

Montgomery County borders Philadelphia on its southeast side. Its 856,553 residents in the 2020 census make it the third most populous county in Pennsylvania. There were 346,877 housing units, with 70.8 percent of occupied homes owner-occupied and 29.2 percent rented.

The county has 22 operating school districts, including Abington, Boyertown Area, Cheltenham, Colonial, Hatboro-Horsham, Jenkintown, Lower Merion, Methacton, Norristown Area, North Penn, Pottstown, Souderton Area, Upper Merion Area, Wissahickon and Spring-Ford Area, plus Bryn Athyn, which exists as an entity but runs no schools. The district that serves a house affects its tax bill and often how buyers weigh it, so name it in your listing.

Selling with unpaid property tax

Start with the bill. Find out which taxing body is owed, since county, municipal and school balances are separate, and ask the Tax Claim Bureau whether the parcel has been returned to it. A parcel that has reached the Bureau can end up at an upset sale once the taxes from two years earlier remain unpaid.

If a sale is scheduled for the parcel, ask the Bureau what must be paid to take it off the list. The Board's forms page also lists homestead and exemption applications, so ask the Board whether the property qualifies and file by the August 1 date.

Ask the closing agent to order a payoff figure early, since interest and costs grow while a parcel sits in the Bureau's hands, and a buyer's lender will want the balance cleared before it funds. Keep copies of any payment receipts so the title company can match them to the parcel.

If time is short, you can sell the house before the Bureau does. That route keeps the deed in your hands and lets the closing pay the tax from the proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

What is the deadline for a Montgomery County assessment appeal?

August 1 is the annual filing deadline, and it applies to tax exemption applications too. Hearings are to be finished by October 31, and results must reach owners and taxing districts by November 15.

Where is the Montgomery County Board of Assessment Appeals?

In Norristown. Mail goes to P.O. Box 311, Norristown, PA 19404-0311, the phone is 610-278-3761, and in-person filings are accepted from 8:30 to 4:00 on weekdays.

Does Montgomery County sell homes for unpaid taxes?

Yes. The Tax Claim Bureau sells delinquent parcels at upset, private, judicial and repository sales. Upset sales are held each September and December, and judicial sales at least once a year in August and December.

Do buyers at a Montgomery County upset sale take on liens?

Yes, at upset and private sales, where the buyer assumes responsibility for all liens. Parcels at a judicial sale are offered free and clear of liens.

Can I mail a Montgomery County appeal on August 1?

Only with proof of the mailing date. Use a hand-cancelled postmark, certificate of mailing, registered or certified mail, or counter-purchased postage, or deliver it by hand in Norristown.

Who sends the tax bill

A Bucks County house is taxed three ways: by the township or borough, by the school district and by the county. Each levy is the assessed value times that year's millage rate, so one parcel can carry three separate charges. County and township bills go out in early March. School district bills follow in early July.

New construction or another change in assessment triggers an interim bill. Interim bills come quarterly on top of the two annual ones. Every municipality has its own elected tax collector, and the county keeps an online directory of them.

Assessed value is set by a different office. The three-member Board of Assessment Appeals determines market value for each parcel, prepares the tax rolls, keeps the tax maps, assigns parcel numbers and labels documents headed for recording. Millage is decided by the taxing bodies, not by the Board.

Bucks County housing context

Bucks is a large, mostly suburban county on the Delaware River, and home prices run well above those in the state's rural counties. It covers 622 square miles with Doylestown as the seat. Lower Bucks is flat and close to Philadelphia and Trenton, while Upper Bucks is hillier farm and village country. Newer building has pushed north through Middletown, Lower Makefield, Northampton and Newtown.

Figures for 2020 to 2024 show 249,187 households, a median home value of $445,700, median household income of $114,764 and an owner-occupied rate of 77.8%. Median gross rent is $1,605. With values at that level, a tax line on a settlement statement deserves a close read, and new construction nearby can bring interim assessments to neighbors.

How to appeal your assessment

File an appeal form with the Board of Assessment Appeals, 55 East Court Street, 6th floor, Doylestown. The filing fee is $75.00 per parcel and is non-refundable. The annual deadline falls in early August and is counted by postmark or office receipt. In 2026 it was August 3. A change won in that round applies the following tax year. Check the county's appeal page each summer for the next date.

Residential appeals follow written rules. Faxed filings are rejected, and a late form is untimely. You, or an attorney holding your signed authorization, must attend the hearing unless you sign a waiver on the form.

  • Evidence of value can be a Pennsylvania certified appraisal that meets USPAP, or sales within the last 18 months of similar homes in your neighborhood.
  • If you bought within 18 months, attach your settlement sheet. It can't be your only evidence.
  • The hearing notice is mailed 20 days ahead, and postponements are refused.
  • A no-show counts as abandoning the appeal, and the fee stays with the county.
  • Group appeals must go through an attorney.

The Board meets on the first and third Tuesday of each month at 10 a.m. at the courthouse in Doylestown. Interim appeals, which follow a revision notice, use the deadline printed on the notice and carry the same $75.00 fee.

Homestead exclusion and tax relief

School districts cut the assessed value of an owner's primary residence through the homestead exclusion. Farm buildings on at least ten contiguous acres can qualify for a farmstead exclusion. For the school tax year that starts July 1, 2027, the application is due to the Board of Assessment Appeals by March 1, 2027. If no form arrived in the mail, download one from the county's page.

You may be asked to prove residency with a driver's license, voter registration or a tax return. A false statement can cost you back taxes with interest, a 10% penalty on the unpaid tax and a fine of up to $2,500. Each year by December 31, school districts must notify an owner whose approval is expiring or was denied.

Older and disabled owners should also look at the state Property Tax/Rent Rebate Program. It pays $380 to $1,000 depending on income and requires household income of $48,110 or less. The deadline for the 2025 claim year is December 31, 2026. The Department of Revenue's help line is 1-888-222-9190.

When taxes go unpaid

Unpaid taxes become a lien, and after 18 months the Tax Claim Bureau can sell the property. Local collectors pass delinquent accounts to the Bureau after December 31, and the Bureau mails a Notice of Claim, usually by certified mail the following spring. The lien is automatic and shows in the public record with no filing at the prothonotary.

The upset sale happens in September of the second year after the first bill. Properties that don't sell move to a continued upset sale and a judicial sale in December, both run online through GovEase. The December 8, 2026 lists are posted on the county's Upset and Judicial Sales page.

  • An Agreement to Stay Sale sets quarterly payments over 12 months for owners facing a sale.
  • After June 1 of the sale year, pay by cashier's check or money order. Taxes 18 months delinquent need certified funds.
  • Cash is no longer taken. The Bureau is at 55 East Court Street, 5th floor, and answers at 215-348-6274 from 8:15 a.m. to 4:15 p.m. on weekdays.

Taxes at closing

Any county, township or school tax debt comes out of the seller's proceeds ahead of other debts, so a lien shrinks the cash you leave with. Before the settlement date, ask the Tax Claim Bureau for a lien certificate using the request form on the county's site. Watch for interim bills as well, since a recent improvement can add a quarterly charge.

The recorder collects a 2% realty transfer tax at recording, split between the state and local governments, and the purchase agreement decides who pays it. Under Act 29, new owners must give the Board of Assessment their contact information within 30 days of buying. A new recorded deed, a refinance included, also ends the homestead exclusion until a fresh application is filed within 45 days.

If you carry tax debt, an expired homestead or a stalled appeal, you can still sell without fixing each item first. A buyer purchasing as-is can close cleanly with the lien paid from proceeds. Get written figures from the Board and the Bureau before you accept any offer.

What to gather before you list

Pull your latest county, township and school bills and check each one against the tax collector's records. Look for any interim bill from a recent improvement. Confirm that the homestead exclusion is active on your primary residence. If you plan to appeal, line up a certified appraisal or recent comparable sales before the deadline, because the hearing notice gives you only 20 days. Then call the Board at 215-348-6219 with any parcel, municipality or school district questions, and request the lien certificate early so the closing agent has it in hand.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I call about a Bucks County assessment?

Call the Board of Assessment Appeals at 215-348-6219. The office is at 55 East Court Street, 6th floor, Doylestown, open 8:30 a.m. to 4:15 p.m., Monday through Friday. Questions about parcel number, municipality or school district go to the same line.

When is the Bucks County homestead exclusion application due?

The application for the school tax year starting July 1, 2027 is due March 1, 2027. File it with the Board of Assessment Appeals. A new recorded deed, including a refinance, requires a new application within 45 days.

What is the filing fee for a Bucks County assessment appeal?

The fee is $75.00 per parcel and it is non-refundable. It applies to annual and interim residential appeals, and the check is payable to the Bucks County Board of Assessment. Don't mail cash.

How long before Bucks County can sell a house for unpaid taxes?

The Tax Claim Bureau can sell a property once a lien stays unpaid for 18 months. Eligible properties go to the upset sale in September of the second year, and unsold ones can move to the December judicial sale. You can stop a sale by paying before the close of business at the courthouse the day before it.

Is there a transfer tax when I sell my Bucks County house?

Yes, a 2% realty transfer tax is paid when the deed is recorded, with 1% to the state and 1% to the municipality and school district. The purchase agreement usually divides it between buyer and seller. Exemptions exist for some family transfers.

The county has about 200,000 billable properties. Mortgage companies and banks pay 35% of county tax, and owners mail in the other 65%.

Each parcel has an 11 digit number. In the county's own example, 34-00-05432-01, the first two digits identify the township or borough, here Nether Providence. Keep your number handy for any call about a bill.

Due dates and discounts

County bills go out February 1 for the calendar year, with a 2% discount available at the start. The discount ends April 1, the face amount is due through June 1, and a 10% penalty applies from then to the end of the year.

How to appeal your assessment

Annual appeals are due August 1 of the year before the year being appealed. The Board of Assessment Appeals must receive them by hand or see a postmark of that day. Fax and email filings are refused. The Board is at the Government Center, 201 West Front Street, Media, PA 19063.

Deferral is a lien, not forgiveness. The deferred amount comes due when the home is sold, when title passes by will or law, or at the owner's death. A surviving co-owner who stays in the home is not forced to pay.

Deferred tax has to be paid before the house is conveyed, so a seller in the deferral program should ask the Treasurer for the balance well before closing. Market value under that program is the assessed value divided by the State Tax Equalization Board's common level ratio for the county.

The estimated population was 580,937 in July 2025, packed into 183.82 square miles. There are 230,160 housing units, and 69.6% are owner-occupied. August 1 of the year before the year being appealed. Appeals must be hand delivered or postmarked by that date, with an original signature and a $50 residential fee. Fax and email are refused.

Yes, 2% off if the county bill is paid by April 1, with bills mailed February 1. The face amount is due from April 2 through June 1, and a 10% penalty applies after that until December 31.

Possibly. The 2026 deferral program covers increases in county tax for owners with household income up to $48,110 who live in the home. The deferred amount is due when the home sells or changes title.

Who sets and collects property tax

Three layers of government share the bill. The county, one of 14 school districts and, in most places, one of the 73 municipalities each levy a tax. The County Assessment Office puts a value on every parcel those levies are applied to. Delinquent bills are the job of the Tax Claim Bureau, which answers to the county commissioners.

State-certified assessors set the values. Whenever an assessment is created or changed, the owner is mailed a Change in Assessment notice, and school districts and municipalities get the same data so they can bill the new amount. The Assessment Office is at 313 W. Market St., Suite 4202, West Chester, phone 610-344-6105, open Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

How a tax bill is calculated

The formula is assessment times millage. A mill is one-thousandth of assessed value, so a rate of 5.164 mills equals 0.005164.

In Chester County the assessment equals 100% of appraised market value as of the base year. The last countywide reassessment took effect for 1998, and the Common Level Ratio exists to account for the gap between assessments and current sale prices. When the Assessment Office prices new work, it uses the computer-assisted mass appraisal model built before that reassessment, and it can't apply the Common Level Ratio to its own figures. Elected officials vote millage rates by dividing the budget by the tax base, so county, school and municipal rates differ by address. Ask the Assessment Office or your municipality for the rates on your parcel.

Appeal deadlines and fees

An annual appeal runs from May 1 through the first business day in August, and the same window covers exemption appeals. A Board decision on an annual appeal doesn't change your bill until the following tax year.

What happens at the hearing

A three-member Board of Assessment Appeals, appointed by the county commissioners for four-year terms, hears each case. Notices go out at least 20 days ahead, and hearings are held at the Government Services Center, 601 Westtown Rd., West Goshen Township.

  • Bring recent photographs of the front and rear of the house, taken within the last six months.
  • Bring appraisals or sale records for similar homes nearby.
  • If you can't attend, send someone with a letter of authorization. Only one of several joint owners needs to appear.

The Board decides a fair market value and then applies the Common Level Ratio, set at 30.6% for annual appeals heard in 2026, with decisions effective for tax bills issued in 2027. Written decisions normally arrive within three to four weeks, though annual appeal results aren't mailed until after August 1. If you disagree, you can go to the Court of Common Pleas within 30 days of the Board's notice.

Homestead exclusion and Clean and Green

The Homestead and Farmstead Exclusion lowers the assessed value of an owner-occupied home, though not a rental or business-only property. Enrollment runs December 15 through the first business day in March, with no fee. Approval isn't automatic. The exclusion shows as a line on the bill, and an approved owner can't be made to reapply more than once every three years. If you move, apply again for the new home.

The Clean and Green program under Act 319 takes applications from March 1 through June 1, filed with the Assessment Office. If you improve a house, know about interim assessments too: a new addition, pool, garage or shed raises the assessment from the first month after completion, and the taxing authorities then bill the increase.

What happens when taxes go unpaid

Taxes are due by December 31 of the year they're levied, and whatever is unpaid after that is delinquent. Taxing authorities certify unpaid liens to the Tax Claim Bureau by January 15, and return and claim notices go out by certified mail by July 31. The bureau works under the Real Estate Tax Sale Law, Act 542 of 1947.

  • The sale is advertised at least 30 days ahead, and a second notice goes by first class mail at least 10 days before.

  • The court must confirm the sale absolute, a step that takes about four to six months before funds are paid out.
  • An unsold property becomes eligible for a judicial sale, which sells it free and clear of liens and mortgages.

Owners can head off a sale with an agreement requiring at least 25% down and three equal installments, or a deferral of up to twelve months. The bureau grants both at its discretion.

The median owner-occupied value is $485,600 for 2020 to 2024, median household income is $127,208 and owner-occupancy is 75.1%. At those values, even a small gap between assessed and market value can make an appeal worthwhile.

If you carry unpaid tax, call both the Tax Claim Bureau and the Assessment Office. Ask each for the current balance and any interim assessment pending on the parcel before you agree to a closing date. Municipal permit offices hand owners a county letter explaining that improvements are assessed, and a certified Pennsylvania evaluator visits to collect property data. A buyer's lender will want the billing history clean, so settle any pending interim notice early.

Steps before you list

Pull your latest bills and your Change in Assessment notices. Check whether the homestead exclusion is on the bill. If an annual appeal window is open, gather photographs and comparable sales. Call the Assessment Office at 610-344-6105 about any pending interim assessment, and the Tax Claim Bureau about any balance. Then give your closing agent the figures in writing so nothing surfaces on settlement day.

What is the deadline to appeal a Chester County property assessment?

Annual appeals may be filed from May 1 through the first business day in August. Interim appeals after new construction must be filed within 40 days of the Change in Assessment notice.

How much does a Chester County assessment appeal cost?

A residential appeal costs $25, a Clean and Green or Act 515 parcel costs $50, and commercial, industrial and exemption appeals cost $150. The fee is paid at filing and isn't refunded.

When does Chester County property tax become delinquent?

Taxes become delinquent after December 31 of the year they are levied. Unpaid taxes can lead to an upset sale held between the second Monday of September and September 30 of the following year.

Can I stop a Chester County tax sale?

Possibly. The Tax Claim Bureau can offer an agreement with 25% down and three equal installments, or a deferral of up to twelve months. Both options are discretionary, so call the bureau before the sale.

Apply to the Assessment-Homestead Office between December 15 and the first business day in March. There is no filing fee, and approval isn't automatic for owner-occupied homes.

Pull your property record from the county site first, since it is free. Next, compare the assessed value with what you expect to list at. If the two are far apart, think about whether a change of assessment notice or a future appeal makes sense, keeping the deadlines above in mind.

It depends on the type. Annual appeals carry a fee that varies by property class, charged per parcel. Change of assessment appeals have no fee, and reassessment appeals are free in the year notices are mailed.

Not automatically. The county, municipalities and school districts must adjust their millage so reassessment does not increase their income. Final rates are set later, and any rate change is a separate decision by each taxing body.

The Treasurer's office at 150 North Queen Street, Suite 122, takes payments, and the county site has an option to pay the county tax bill online. Call 717-299-8222 for hours that suit your schedule.

Westmoreland County tax offices

Three county offices share the work. One decides what your property is worth, one feeds data to the local collectors, and one chases unpaid bills. Expect weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

Tax Assessment certifies the value of every parcel, and the county, schools and municipalities all send bills based on it. Its staff look over building and demolition permits from each municipality, inspect new construction, and send you a notice when a value changes. Visit Suite 440 at 40 North Pennsylvania Avenue, Greensburg, PA 15601.

Each local tax collector gets that year's real estate data from the Tax Office. Anything unpaid from a prior year moves to the Tax Claim Bureau, a body set up by state law that collects delinquent county, municipal and school taxes and holds the sales. Call it at 724-830-3428.

Who collects delinquent tax

The Tax Claim Bureau covers 65 districts, but nine places are exceptions: the City of Greensburg, Hempfield Township, Irwin Borough, the City of Latrobe, North Huntingdon Township, Penn Township, Trafford Borough, Jeannette School District and Monessen School District.

A house in any of those places has its back taxes handled locally, by the collector or the municipality. The county bureau is not involved. Work out who holds the claim before you trust any payoff number.

  • Covered district: phone the bureau on 724-830-3428.
  • Excepted district: request the balance from the municipal or school tax office.
  • Insist on a written payoff that shows a good-through date, so the title company can settle it from the sale.

How to appeal your assessment

Take your case to the Board of Assessment Appeals. A change-of-assessment notice gives you 40 days from its mailing date. Outside that, any owner can appeal once a year, by August 1, and a win applies from the next tax year.

Get the form online under Forms or pick one up at Tax Assessment. Your signed copy has to arrive by August 1, and the office will not take a fax or an email. Hearings are held on the second Thursday of every month, 9:00 a.m., fourth floor, Suite 440.

Selling soon? An appeal filed by August 1 only changes the following year's bill, so ask the closing agent how this year's bill will be prorated at closing.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Westmoreland County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Tax sales: upset and judicial

Unpaid taxes can lead to two auctions. The upset sale comes first, and a judicial sale follows for anything that does not sell. Only parcels two or more years behind are put up, and the goal is to get them paying taxes again.

The upset sale is held each September at 10:00 a.m. in the Commissioners Meeting Rooms of the Courthouse Annex. The judicial sale comes later, in the first-floor Public Meeting Rooms of the Courthouse, and the county fixes new dates every year. Act 33 makes bidders register at least 10 days ahead, and a judicial sale needs registration in person.

Property bought at a judicial sale comes free and clear of taxes, liens, mortgages and judgments, except federal government liens. The high bidder owes the bid plus costs: a $110.25 deed recording fee, 2 percent transfer tax on assessed value and a $25.00 deed preparation fee. Whatever does not sell lands in a repository file and is not taxed until a buyer appears.

Staying out of a tax sale

Frequently, through a payment agreement, when the debt is on your home. Owners two years behind can sign one with the bureau between May 1 and the Friday before the September sale. A call to 724-830-3428 will tell you whether you qualify.

The bureau will not take a personal check. It accepts cash, money orders, cashier's or certified checks, and online payments, which add 1.00 percent on personal debit cards or 2.60 percent on personal credit cards. Card payments close earlier than counter payments, which run until the Friday before the sale, and nothing is taken on sale day.

Millage rates change by municipality and school district. Ask the Tax Office for the rate that applies to your parcel, since there is no single countywide number.

Westmoreland County housing at a glance

Westmoreland sits near Pittsburgh and has about 349,324 residents in 154,979 households. Owners live in 78.4 percent of homes, at a median value of $203,500, and mortgage holders pay a median $1,452 monthly. A Land Bank and Development Authority acquires vacant, abandoned and tax-delinquent houses, which is where a neglected house with back taxes may land.

Selling a house with back taxes

First find the claim holder, either the bureau or, in the nine excepted places, the local collector. Get the payoff in writing and hand it to your attorney or title company, who deducts the balance from your proceeds and clears the record.

With two years owed, the agreement window may still be open, and using it before the September sale can buy time. A cash buyer can close fast and pay the taxes at the table without waiting on a lender's appraisal, but the payoff steps stay the same.

What to gather before you list

A little paperwork up front saves trouble at closing. Pull your latest tax bills and note the parcel, the municipality and the school district, since those three decide which collector you deal with and what the millage is. If you ever received a notice of changed assessment, keep it, because it shows the date the 40-day appeal window began.

Then call the Tax Assessment office to confirm the value on file and to ask whether any building or demolition permit has changed it. If a permit is open or a past project was never reported, better to learn that before a buyer's inspector does. Finally, ask the right office, the Tax Claim Bureau or your local collector, whether anything is owed for earlier years. A clean answer in writing makes the sale simpler.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Westmoreland County assessment appeal deadline?

Each August 1, for a result that starts the next tax year. If you receive a notice of changed assessment, you get 40 days from its mailing instead. Filing is at the Board of Assessment Appeals, Suite 440, Greensburg.

Who do I call about delinquent taxes in Westmoreland County?

Try the Tax Claim Bureau, 724-830-3428. 65 districts use it, while Greensburg, Hempfield Township and a few others collect on their own.

Can I pay delinquent Westmoreland County taxes by personal check?

No personal checks. Use cash, a money order, a cashier's or certified check, or pay online, where debit costs 1.00 percent extra and credit 2.60 percent.

How many years behind triggers a Westmoreland County tax sale?

Two years or more. Such parcels are offered at the yearly upset sale and, if unsold, at a judicial sale, where bidders register in person at least 10 days ahead.

Does a Westmoreland County tax sale wipe out mortgages?

A judicial sale clears taxes, liens, mortgages and judgments, except U.S. government liens. At an upset sale liens may survive, so buyers should order a title search.

County offices that handle property tax

Two county offices matter most. The Assessment Office sets the value your tax bill is built on. The Revenue and Tax Claim Bureau collects delinquent taxes. Both work from the Erie County Courthouse, 140 West Sixth Street, Erie, PA 16501. Appeals go to Room 104, and delinquent taxes are paid in Room 110.

The Assessment Office assesses all real estate in the county and runs the various tax programs. The Tax Claim Bureau is one of four divisions of the county Department of Finance. It collects delinquent taxes for the county, the City of Erie and the other municipalities, and the school districts, then passes the money out to each of them every month.

Local tax collectors bill current-year taxes. To learn what is due for the year of a sale, ask the tax collector for your municipality rather than the county.

How to appeal your assessment

File a Notice of Intention to Appeal Property Assessment with the Erie County Board of Appeals, and make sure it arrives between January 1 and August 1. Hearings run from July through October.

  • Use one form for each parcel.
  • Include the county parcel ID, the property location, your own estimate of value and the reason for the appeal.
  • List up to three comparable properties that sold recently or are listed for sale, by county index number, name and address.
  • Pay the non-refundable filing fee with a check made out to County of Erie.

County Council Ordinance No. 157 of 2007 sets the fee. The form cautions that comparable assessments are not treated as an indication of fair market value, and an exterior photograph of the property is available at the hearing.

Filing opens your property to revaluation, so the assessment can go down, go up or stay put. Weigh that before you file on a house you plan to sell soon. If a corporation owns the house, an officer signs the form. The county also has a Catastrophic Loss Appeal form for damage cases.

Exemptions and ownership forms

The Assessment Office's Documents and Forms page offers applications that change who is taxed or how much. Some matter to a seller, because a change of owner should be reported to the county once the deed is done.

  • Application for Homestead and Farmstead Exclusions
  • Application for Exemption From Erie County Real Property Taxes
  • Owner Change Form and Owner Registry Form
  • Clean and Green application, Clean and Green information and the Act 319 Notice of Conveyance
  • Mobile Home Change of Ownership Form
  • Change of Address form

Clean and Green land has its own notice at conveyance, so a buyer of a farm parcel should review that form before closing. Millage rate charts for each year back to 2011 are posted, with a revised chart for 2026. Rates differ by municipality and school district, so use the chart that matches your house.

Tax sale and fees

The Tax Claim Bureau holds an upset sale online through GovEase for parcels whose taxes are at least two years delinquent. Bidders pre-register, the winning bid is paid in full by 3:30 p.m. on sale day, and parcels that do not sell can move to a later judicial sale run by a law firm.

The minimum bid is roughly the delinquent and current taxes plus municipal liens. The owner of a property headed to the judicial sale may not bid on it.

Stopping a sale or paying delinquent taxes

An owner can stop a sale. Even after a bid is made at the upset sale, the owner can pay the delinquency before the winning bidder pays the upset price, and the property is treated as if it had never been offered. Once the bidder pays in full, there is no redemption period.

Delinquent taxes are paid in Room 110 of the courthouse, Monday through Friday from 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM. The office is closed on county holidays. It takes cash, attorney IOLTA checks, money orders, certified checks, business or personal checks and MasterCard or Visa. Online payments carry an extra fee of usually around 3%. Interest and costs are added from time to time, so call the Bureau at 814-451-6206 for a current figure.

A stay of sale agreement works as an installment plan, but it cannot be set up online.

  • An owner named on the deed appears in person with state-issued ID or a passport.
  • The down payment is at least 25% of the most recent two years of delinquent taxes.
  • Any older unpaid taxes must be paid in full.
  • A default bars a new installment agreement for three years.

Selling with taxes owed

You can sell as long as the delinquent balance is paid from the proceeds or before closing. Ask the Tax Claim Bureau for a payoff figure close to the closing date, since interest and costs keep accruing, and ask your municipality's tax collector for the amount on the current year's bill.

A house already in the sale process is harder. The owner of a property headed to the judicial or repository sale cannot bid on it, and repository sales carry no right of redemption. If your house is on a published list, talk to the Bureau about a stay of sale before you sign a contract, since that may buy time for a closing.

The buyer's side matters too. Liens, judgments and rents of record follow a property, which is why tax sale bidders are told to order a title search. A buyer's title agent will do the same on an ordinary sale and will insist that anything found is paid off. A cash buyer will still want taxes settled, so get the payoff in writing.

Erie County housing

The median value of owner-occupied homes in Erie County is $177,000 for 2020 to 2024, and 68.1% of homes are owner-occupied. There are 110,587 households and median household income is $63,354. Owners with a mortgage have median monthly costs of $1,393, those without a mortgage $572, and median gross rent is $904. The county issued 243 building permits in 2025.

Frequently asked questions

When can I file an assessment appeal in Erie County?

Appeal forms are accepted from January 1 through August 1. Hearings run from July through October.

How much does it cost to appeal an Erie County assessment?

The non-refundable filing fee is $50.00 for the main parcel plus $10.00 for each additional parcel that makes up the property. Checks are made out to County of Erie.

Where do I pay delinquent property taxes in Erie County?

Pay in Room 110 of the Erie County Courthouse, 140 West Sixth Street, Monday through Friday from 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM. You can also pay online from the parcel's tax page, with an added fee of usually around 3%.

What is a stay of sale agreement in Erie County?

It is an installment plan that keeps a delinquent property out of a tax sale. It needs at least 25% of the last two years of delinquent taxes down, payment of all older taxes, and an owner on the deed appearing in person with photo ID.

Can the owner buy back a house after an Erie County upset sale?

Not after the sale is complete. The owner can pay the delinquency before the winning bidder pays the upset price, but once the bidder pays in full by 3:30 p.m. on sale day there is no period of redemption.
